claim: RNA granules are non-membrane bound cellular compartments that contain RNA and RNA binding proteins.
source: RNA granules are non-membrane bound cellular compartments that contain RNA and RNA binding proteins.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about RNA granules.

claim: During polarization of the C. elegans zygote, germline RNA granules, called P granules, assemble preferentially in the posterior cytoplasm.
source: During polarization of the C. elegans zygote, germline RNA granules, called P granules, assemble preferentially in the posterior cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a well-established observation in the field, supported by the authors' own data shown in Figure 1.

claim: P granule asymmetry depends on RNA-induced phase separation of the granule scaffold MEG-3.
source: We present evidence that P granule asymmetry depends on RNA-induced phase separation of the granule scaffold MEG-3.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple in vitro and in vivo experiments shown in Figures 3-5.

claim: MEG-3 is an intrinsically disordered protein that binds and phase separates with RNA in vitro.
source: MEG-3 is an intrinsically disordered protein that binds and phase separates with RNA in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing MEG-3 has a predicted IDR, binds poly-U30 RNA (Figure 3), and forms phase-separated condensates with RNA (Figure 4).

claim: MEG-3 forms a posterior-rich concentration gradient that is anti-correlated with a gradient in the RNA-binding protein MEX-5.
source: In vivo, MEG-3 forms a posterior-rich concentration gradient that is anti-correlated with a gradient in the RNA-binding protein MEX-5.
evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging data shown in Figure 1A and quantified in Figure 1B.

claim: MEX-5 is necessary and sufficient to suppress MEG-3 granule formation in vivo.
source: MEX-5 is necessary and sufficient to suppress MEG-3 granule formation in vivo
evidence: This is supported by genetic experiments showing that loss of MEX-5/6 leads to uniform MEG-3 granules (Figure 1C) and uniform MEX-5 prevents MEG-3 granule formation (Figure 2B).

claim: MEX-5 suppresses RNA-induced MEG-3 phase separation in vitro.
source: MEX-5 is necessary and sufficient to suppress MEG-3 granule formation in vivo, and suppresses RNA-induced MEG-3 phase separation in vitro.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro phase separation assays shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: MEX-5 interferes with MEG-3's access to RNA, thus locally suppressing MEG-3 phase separation to drive P granule asymmetry.
source: Our findings suggest that MEX-5 interferes with MEG-3's access to RNA, thus locally suppressing MEG-3 phase separation to drive P granule asymmetry.
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on inference from their in vitro and in vivo experimental data.

claim: Regulated access to RNA, combined with RNA-induced phase separation of key scaffolding proteins, may be a general mechanism for controlling the formation of RNA granules in space and time.
source: Regulated access to RNA, combined with RNA-induced phase separation of key scaffolding proteins, may be a general mechanism for controlling the formation of RNA granules in space and time.
evidence: This is a speculative generalization of the findings to other RNA granule systems.

claim: Cytoplasmic RNA granule components typically exchange rapidly between a highly concentrated pool in the granule and a more diffuse, less concentrated pool in the cytoplasm.
source: Cytoplasmic RNA granule components typically exchange rapidly between a highly concentrated pool in the granule and a more diffuse, less concentrated pool in the cytoplasm (Weber and Brangwynne, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Weber and Brangwynne, 2012.

claim: Proteins in RNA granules often contain prion-like, low complexity, or intrinsically-disordered regions (IDRs).
source: In addition to RNA-binding domains, proteins in RNA granules often contain prion-like, low complexity, or intrinsically-disordered regions (IDRs) (Courchaine, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Courchaine, 2016.

claim: In concentrated solutions, IDRs spontaneously de-mix from the aqueous solvent to form liquid droplets (liquid-liquid phase separation or LLPS) or hydrogels.
source: In concentrated solutions, IDRs spontaneously de-mix from the aqueous solvent to form liquid droplets (liquid-liquid phase separation or LLPS) or hydrogels (Li et al., 2012; Weber and Brangwynne, 2012; Elbaum-Garfinkle et al., 2015; Guo and Shorter, 2015; Lin et al., 2015; Nott et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Proteins in LLPS droplets and hydrogels exchange with the solvent.
source: Like RNA granules in vivo, proteins in LLPS droplets and hydrogels exchange with the solvent (Kato et al., 2012; Li et al., 2012; Elbaum-Garfinkle et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: LLPS or reversible gelation drives the assembly of RNA granules in vivo.
source: These findings have suggested that LLPS or reversible gelation drives the assembly of RNA granules in vivo (Guo and Shorter, 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the field, supported by citation to Guo and Shorter, 2015.

claim: Stress granules assemble within seconds of exposure to toxic stimulants that require the temporary removal of mRNAs from the translational pool.
source: For example, stress granules assemble within seconds of exposure to toxic stimulants that require the temporary removal of mRNAs from the translational pool (Anderson and Kedersha, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Anderson and Kedersha, 2006.

claim: In eggs, germ granules assemble in the germ plasm, a specialized area of the cytoplasm that is partitioned to the nascent germline during the first embryonic cleavages.
source: In eggs, germ granules assemble in the germ plasm, a specialized area of the cytoplasm that is partitioned to the nascent germline during the first embryonic cleavages (Voronina et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Voronina et al., 2011.

claim: For most of development, P granules are stable perinuclear structures, but in the transition from oocyte-to-embryo, P granules detach from the nucleus and become highly dynamic.
source: For most of development, P granules are stable perinuclear structures, but in the transition from oocyte-to-embryo, P granules detach from the nucleus and become highly dynamic (Pitt et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pitt et al., 2000 and Wang et al., 2014.

claim: As the oocyte is ovulated in the spermatheca, P granules disassemble and release their components in the cytoplasm.
source: As the oocyte is ovulated in the spermatheca, P granules disassemble and release their components in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a known observation in the field, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: After fertilization, P granule proteins reassemble into dynamic granules that undergo repeated cycles of assembly and disassembly in synchrony with cell division.
source: After fertilization, P granule proteins reassemble into dynamic granules that undergo repeated cycles of assembly and disassembly in synchrony with cell division.
evidence: This is a known observation in the field, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: Live imaging in the 1-cell zygote has revealed that these cycles are spatially patterned along the anterior-posterior axis of the embryo: granule assembly is favored in the posterior and granule disassembly is favored in the anterior.
source: Live imaging in the 1-cell zygote has revealed that these cycles are spatially patterned along the anterior-posterior axis of the embryo: granule assembly is favored in the posterior and granule disassembly is favored in the anterior (Brangwynne et al., 2009; Gallo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brangwynne et al., 2009 and Gallo et al., 2010.

claim: By the first mitosis, P granules are found exclusively in the posterior cytoplasm together with other germ plasm components.
source: By the first mitosis, P granules are found exclusively in the posterior cytoplasm together with other germ plasm components.
evidence: This is a known observation in the field, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: P granules are segregated to the posterior germline blastomere P1 and excluded from the anterior somatic blastomere AB.
source: As a result, P granules are segregated to the posterior germline blastomere P1 and excluded from the anterior somatic blastomere AB.
evidence: This is a known observation in the field, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: P granule asymmetry is under the control of the PAR polarity network which divides the zygote into distinct anterior and posterior domains.
source: P granule asymmetry is under the control of the PAR polarity network which divides the zygote into distinct anterior and posterior domains (Motegi and Seydoux, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Motegi and Seydoux, 2013.

claim: The PAR-1 kinase is enriched in the posterior cytoplasm and restricts the RNA-binding protein MEX-5 (and its redundant homolog MEX-6) to the anterior cytoplasm.
source: The PAR-1 kinase is enriched in the posterior cytoplasm and restricts the RNA-binding protein MEX-5 (and its redundant homolog MEX-6) to the anterior cytoplasm (Griffin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Griffin et al., 2011.

claim: MEX-5 and MEX-6 restrict P granules to the posterior.
source: MEX-5 and MEX-6 in turn restrict P granules to the posterior (Schubert et al., 2000; Gallo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schubert et al., 2000 and Gallo et al., 2010.

claim: In mex-5 mex-6 double mutants, P granule still undergo cycles of assembly and disassembly but these are no longer patterned along the anterior-posterior axis, and small granules remain throughout the cytoplasm.
source: In mex-5 mex-6 double mutants, P granule still undergo cycles of assembly and disassembly but these are no longer patterned along the anterior-posterior axis, and small granules remain throughout the cytoplasm (Gallo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gallo et al., 2010.

claim: MEX-5 blocks phase separation of P granule components in the anterior cytoplasm.
source: An attractive hypothesis is that MEX-5 blocks phase separation of P granule components in the anterior cytoplasm (Brangwynne et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the field, supported by citations to Brangwynne et al., 2009 and Lee et al., 2013.

claim: P granule assembly in zygotes requires several P granule proteins, including the RNA-binding protein PGL-1 (and its redundant paralog PGL-3) and the intrinsically-disordered protein MEG-3 (and its redundant paralog MEG-4).
source: P granule assembly in zygotes requires several P granule proteins, including the RNA-binding protein PGL-1 (and its redundant paralog PGL-3) and the intrinsically-disordered protein MEG-3 (and its redundant paralog MEG-4) (Hanazawa et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hanazawa et al., 2011 and Wang et al., 2014.

claim: PGL-1 and PGL-3 are RGG domain proteins that self-associate and recruit other RNA-binding proteins to the granules, including the GLH family of RNA helicases.
source: PGL-1 and PGL-3 are RGG domain proteins that self-associate and recruit other RNA-binding proteins to the granules, including the GLH family of RNA helicases (Updike and Strome, 2010; Hanazawa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Updike and Strome, 2010 and Hanazawa et al., 2011.

claim: MEG-3 and MEG-4 are redundant, serine-rich proteins that bind to PGL-1 in vitro and are essential for P granule assembly in embryos.
source: MEG-3 and MEG-4 are redundant, serine-rich proteins that bind to PGL-1 in vitro and are essential for P granule assembly in embryos.
evidence: This is a known observation from previous work, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: In zygotes lacking meg-3 and meg-4, PGL-1 and GLH-2 form transient assemblies that do not segregate asymmetrically and are not maintained in later stages.
source: In zygotes lacking meg-3 and meg-4, PGL-1 and GLH-2 form transient assemblies that do not segregate asymmetrically and are not maintained in later stages (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: Phosphorylation of MEG-3 by the DYRK kinase MBK-2 promotes granule disassembly in zygotes.
source: Phosphorylation of MEG-3 by the DYRK kinase MBK-2 promotes granule disassembly in zygotes, but the mechanism that favors disassembly specifically in the anterior cytoplasm is not known (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: Before polarization, MEX-5, MEG-3, PGL-1 and GLH-1 were all distributed evenly throughout the cytoplasm.
source: Before polarization, MEX-5, MEG-3, PGL-1 and GLH-1 were all distributed evenly throughout the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: MEX-5 appeared mostly diffuse in the cytoplasm with a few foci before polarization.
source: MEX-5 appeared mostly diffuse in the cytoplasm with a few foci
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: MEG-3, PGL-1, and GLH-1 appeared both diffuse and enriched in many small (<1 micron diameter) foci before polarization.
source: whereas MEG-3, PGL-1, and GLH-1 appeared both diffuse and enriched in many small (<1 micron diameter) foci (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: During polarization (pronuclear formation and migration), MEX-5 and MEG-3 began to redistribute into opposing cytoplasmic gradients along the long axis of the zygote (anterior-posterior axis) with MEG-3 beginning to form large (~1 micron) granules in the posterior.
source: During polarization (pronuclear formation and migration), MEX-5 and MEG-3 began to redistribute into opposing cytoplasmic gradients along the long axis of the zygote (anterior-posterior axis) with MEG-3 beginning to form large (~1 micron) granules in the posterior (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Total levels of MEG-3 do not change during polarization, consistent with redistribution of existing MEG-3 protein from anterior to posterior.
source: Total levels of MEG-3 do not change during this period, consistent with redistribution of existing MEG-3 protein from anterior to posterior (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of MEG-3::meGFP fluorescence shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In contrast to MEX-5 and MEG-3, PGL-1 and GLH-1 remained uniformly distributed during polarization.
source: In contrast to MEX-5 and MEG-3, PGL-1 and GLH-1 remained uniformly distributed during polarization.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: After polarization (mitosis), all proteins were localized, with MEX-5 in the anterior cytoplasm and MEG-3, PGL-1 and GLH-1 in large granules in the posterior cytoplasm.
source: After polarization (mitosis), all proteins were localized, with MEX-5 in the anterior cytoplasm and MEG-3, PGL-1 and GLH-1 in large granules in the posterior cytoplasm (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In zygotes derived from mothers treated with double-stranded RNA against mex-5 and mex-6 (mex-5/6(RNAi) zygotes), the MEG-3 gradient did not form and MEG-3 and PGL-1 granules remained uniformly distributed throughout the cytoplasm.
source: In zygotes derived from mothers treated with double-stranded RNA against mex-5 and mex-6 (mex-5/6(RNAi) zygotes), the MEG-3 gradient did not form and MEG-3 and PGL-1 granules remained uniformly distributed throughout the cytoplasm (Figure 1C, (Gallo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1C and citation to Gallo et al., 2010.

claim: In meg-3; meg-4 double mutant embryos, the MEX-5 gradient was unaffected but neither PGL-1 nor PGL-3 granules segregated properly.
source: In meg-3; meg-4 double mutant embryos, the MEX-5 gradient was unaffected but neither PGL-1 nor PGL-3 granules segregated properly (Wang et al., 2014), Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: In pgl-1(RNAi); pgl-3(bn104) zygotes, the MEG-3 and MEG-4 gradients were unaffected and MEG-3/MEG-4 granules formed in the posterior as in wild-type, except that the granules appeared smaller especially in zygotes.
source: In pgl-1(RNAi); pgl-3(bn104) zygotes, the MEG-3 and MEG-4 gradients were unaffected and MEG-3/MEG-4 granules formed in the posterior as in wild-type, except that the granules appeared smaller especially in zygotes (Wang et al., 2014), Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: MEX-5 and MEX-6 regulate granule asymmetry by localizing MEG-3 and MEG-4 to the posterior, which in turn are required to localize PGL-1 and PGL-3.
source: These analyses suggest that MEX-5 and MEX-6 regulate granule asymmetry by localizing MEG-3 and MEG-4 to the posterior, which in turn are required to localize PGL-1 and PGL-3.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the genetic hierarchy experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: PGL-1 and PGL-3 are not required to localize MEG-3 or MEG-4 or to assemble MEG-3/4 granules, but contribute to the size of MEG-3/4 granules.
source: PGL-1 and PGL-3 are not required to localize MEG-3 or MEG-4 or to assemble MEG-3/4 granules, but contribute to the size of MEG-3/4 granules as reported previously (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the genetic hierarchy experiments shown in Figure 1, and supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: The formation of the MEX-5 gradient requires phosphorylation of serine 404 in the C-terminus of MEX-5 by the kinase PAR-1.
source: Using mex-5 transgenes, Griffin et al. (2011) showed that the formation of the MEX-5 gradient requires phosphorylation of serine 404 in the C-terminus of MEX-5 by the kinase PAR-1.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Griffin et al., 2011.

claim: MEX-5(S404A) failed to form a gradient during zygote polarization and remained uniformly distributed.
source: As expected, we found that MEX-5(S404A) failed to form a gradient during zygote polarization and remained uniformly distributed (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In zygotes derived from mothers homozygous for mex-5(s404a) (mex-5(S404A) zygotes), MEG-3 did not form a gradient or granules and remained uniformly distributed in the cytoplasm throughout the 1-cell stage.
source: Using the MEG-3::GFP strain, we found that zygotes derived from mothers homozygous for mex-5(s404a) (mex-5(S404A) zygotes), MEG-3 did not form a gradient or granules. Instead, MEG-3 remained uniformly distributed in the cytoplasm throughout the 1-cell stage (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: MEX-5 is sufficient to suppress the formation of MEG-3 granules throughout the cytoplasm.
source: We conclude that MEX-5 is sufficient to suppress the formation of MEG-3 granules throughout the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the mex-5(S404A) experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mutation of a single amino acid in each finger (R247E and K318E) reduces MEX-5 binding affinity for poly-U by 35-fold.
source: Pagano et al. (2007) have shown that mutation of a single amino acid in each finger (R247E and K318E) reduces MEX-5 binding affinity for poly-U by 35-fold.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pagano et al., 2007.

claim: The finger mutations R247E and K318E disrupt formation of the MEX-5 gradient in vivo.
source: Using mex-5 transgenes, Griffin et al. (2011) showed the finger mutations R247E and K318E also disrupt formation of the MEX-5 gradient in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Griffin et al., 2011.

claim: MEX-5(ZF-) did not form a gradient and was uniformly distributed in zygotes.
source: Like MEX-5(S404A), MEX-5(ZF-) did not form a gradient and was uniformly distributed in zygotes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: mex-5(ZF-) zygotes assembled posterior MEG-3 granules as in wild-type.
source: In contrast to mex-5(S404A) zygotes, however, mex-5(ZF-) zygotes assembled posterior MEG-3 granules as in wild-type (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the authors' experiments.

claim: mex-5 is partially redundant with its paralog, mex-6.
source: mex-5 is partially redundant with its paralog, mex-6 (Schubert et al., 2000), which is sufficient to polarize MEG granules in the absence of MEX-5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schubert et al., 2000 and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Depletion of mex-6 by RNAi in mex-5(ZF-) zygotes caused MEG-3 granules to assemble throughout the cytoplasm, as in mex-5/6(RNAi) zygotes.
source: Consistent with this redundancy, we found that depletion of mex-6 by RNAi in mex-5(ZF-) zygotes caused MEG-3 granules to assemble throughout the cytoplasm, as in mex-5/6(RNAi) zygotes (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: mex-5(ZF-) is a loss-of-function allele.
source: These observations suggest that mex-5(ZF-) is a loss-of-function allele.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the genetic experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The loss of mex-5 activity was not due to reduced expression as MEX-5(ZF-) was expressed at the same level as wild-type MEX-5.
source: The loss of mex-5 activity was not due to reduced expression as MEX-5(ZF-) was expressed at the same level as wild-type MEX-5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: mex-5(ZF-,S404A) zygotes assembled posterior MEG-3::GFP granules, as is observed in mex-5(ZF-) and wild-type zygotes.
source: We found that mex-5(ZF-,S404A) zygotes assembled posterior MEG-3::GFP granules, as is observed in mex-5(ZF-) and wild-type zygotes.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the authors' experiments.

claim: Depletion of mex-6 by RNAi in mex-5(ZF-,S404A) background yielded zygotes with uniform MEG-3::GFP granules, as expected for a mex-5/6 loss-of-function phenotype.
source: Depletion of mex-6 by RNAi in this background yielded zygotes with uniform MEG-3::GFP granules, as expected for a mex-5/6 loss-of-function phenotype (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Suppression of MEG-3 granule assembly by MEX-5 depends on MEX-5's ability to bind RNA with high affinity.
source: We conclude that suppression of MEG-3 granule assembly by MEX-5 depends on MEX-5's ability to bind RNA with high affinity.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the genetic experiments with MEX-5 zinc finger mutants shown in Figure 2.

claim: MEG-3 does not have a recognizable RNA-binding domain.
source: Unlike MEX-5, MEG-3 does not have a recognizable RNA-binding domain (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: MEG-3 contains a long predicted intrinsically-disordered region (IDR) at its N-terminus (aa1-550) followed by a region with lower predicted disorder (aa550-862).
source: MEG-3 contains a long predicted intrinsically-disordered region (IDR) at its N-terminus (aa1-550) followed by a region with lower predicted disorder (aa550-862) [IUPRED predictions, (Dosztányi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on computational predictions using IUPRED, cited to Dosztányi et al., 2005.

claim: MEG-3 and MEG-3IDR interact with poly-U30 RNA to form complexes that migrate as a discrete band during electrophoresis.
source: EMSA experiments revealed that MEG-3 and MEG-3IDR interact with poly-U30 RNA to form complexes that migrate as a discrete band during electrophoresis (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The apparent dissociation constant (Kd,app) of MEG-3 for poly-U30 is ~32 nM, similar to that of MEX-5 (Kd,app= ~ 29 nM).
source: Using FP, we calculated the apparent dissociation constant (Kd,app) of MEG-3 for poly-U30 to be ~32 nM, similar to that of MEX-5 (Kd,app= ~ 29 nM) (Pagano et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization data and citation to Pagano et al., 2007 for MEX-5 Kd.

claim: MEG-3IDR bound RNA with ~15 fold lower affinity (Kd,app= ~ 460 nM) than full-length MEG-3.
source: MEG-3IDR also bound RNA but with ~15 fold lower affinity (Kd,app= ~ 460 nM).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: MEG-3Cterm did not bind RNA significantly by EMSA or in the FP assay (Kd,app > 3000 nM).
source: MEG-3Cterm did not bind RNA significantly by EMSA or in the FP assay (Kd,app > 3000 nM) (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA and fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: MEG-3 binds RNA with high affinity and this activity resides primarily within the MEG-3 IDR, although high affinity binding also requires the MEG-3 C-terminus.
source: We conclude that MEG-3 binds RNA with high affinity and that this activity resides primarily within the MEG-3 IDR, although high affinity binding also requires the MEG-3 C-terminus.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the RNA binding assays shown in Figure 3.

claim: Poly-U, and to a lesser extent poly-A, were effective competitors for MEG-3/poly-U30 complexes, but not poly-C or poly-G.
source: We found that poly-U, and to a lesser extent poly-A, were effective competitors, but not poly-C or poly-G (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA competition EMSA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: MEG-3's affinity for RNA is affected by nucleotide composition.
source: These observations suggest that MEG-3's affinity for RNA is affected by nucleotide composition.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the RNA competition experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Concentrated (<1 μM) solutions of RNA-binding proteins containing IDRs spontaneously phase separate when switched from high to low salt (150 mM NaCl).
source: Concentrated (<1 μM) solutions of RNA-binding proteins containing IDRs spontaneously phase separate when switched from high to low salt (150 mM NaCl) (Elbaum-Garfinkle et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2015; Nott et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MEG-3 and MEG-3IDR readily formed phase-separated condensates within 10 min at room temperature when diluted from 6M urea into aqueous buffer (150 mM NaCl).
source: We found that MEG-3 and MEG-3IDR readily formed phase-separated condensates within 10 min at room temperature.
evidence: This is supported by phase separation assay data described in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Control proteins (BSA and MBP) subjected to the same treatment did not phase separate.
source: Control proteins (BSA and MBP) subjected to the same treatment did not phase separate (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the authors' experiments.

claim: MEG-3 condensates were observed across a range of protein concentrations (0.5 μM to 5 μM) and became larger and more abundant with increasing protein concentration.
source: MEG-3 condensates were observed across a range of protein concentrations (0.5 μM to 5 μM) and became larger and more abundant with increasing protein concentration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by phase separation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: MEG-3 and MEG-3IDR behaved similarly to each other, except that in the low concentration range (<5 μM), MEG-3 formed more condensates than MEG-3IDR, and in the high concentration range (>5 μM) MEG-3IDR tended to form larger condensates.
source: MEG-3 and MEG-3IDR behaved similarly to each other, except that in the low concentration range (<5 μM), MEG-3 formed more condensates than MEG-3IDR, and in the high concentration range (>5 μM) MEG-3IDR tended to form larger condensates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by phase separation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: RNA can stimulate the phase transition of IDR proteins that bind RNA.
source: RNA can stimulate the phase transition of IDR proteins that bind RNA (Guo and Shorter, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo and Shorter, 2015.

claim: 0.1 μM poly-U30 was sufficient to increase the number of visible condensates especially at low MEG-3 protein concentrations (<1 μM).
source: We found that 0.1 μM poly-U30 was sufficient to increase the number of visible condensates especially at low MEG-3 protein concentrations (<1 μM) (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by phase separation assay data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Higher concentrations of RNA increased the number of MEG-3 condensates even further.
source: Higher concentrations of RNA increased the number of MEG-3 condensates even further.
evidence: This is supported by phase separation assay data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: For a given concentration of poly-U30, MEG-3 formed more condensates than MEG-3IDR.
source: For a given concentration of poly-U30, MEG-3 formed more condensates than MEG-3IDR (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by phase separation assay data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Addition of sub-stochiometric amounts of fluorescently tagged poly-U30 confirmed that the RNA phase separates with MEG-3.
source: Addition of sub-stochiometric amounts of fluorescently tagged poly-U30 confirmed that the RNA phase separates with MEG-3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: MEG-3 and MEG-3IDR have an intrinsic propensity to phase separate that can be stimulated by RNA.
source: We conclude that MEG-3 and MEG-3IDR have an intrinsic propensity to phase separate that can be stimulated by RNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the phase separation assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: MEX-5 strongly inhibited MEG-3 phase separation induced by RNA.
source: We found that MEX-5 strongly inhibited MEG-3 phase separation induced by RNA.
evidence: This is supported by phase separation assay data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Addition of excess RNA (3-fold increase) restored robust phase separation in the presence of MEX-5.
